enter_pairing_mode.notes: No source describes how an owner's phone is enrolled. The researchers' recommendation — that a physical action inside the car, such as a button press, be required when a new phone connects — is offered as a fix for systems of this class, which suggests none was needed, but it is not stated for KARR specifically.

pairing.notes: The gate is application-layer, not link-layer: the UC San Diego team's project page says each of the six aftermarket systems it studied runs its own application-layer BLE security protocol, and KARR's authenticates the app with a key shared by every unit. So a connection does need something before the alarm answers — but on unpatched firmware that something is the same for everyone, and anyone who has read it out of the app can unlock, silence and immobilise any car in about five yards. This integration never connects; it matches the advertisement and warns. Low confidence because the protocol details sit in the USENIX Security 2026 paper ("BLE Theft Auto"), which this project could not retrieve, and the researchers deliberately withheld exploit-level detail; what is here comes from the project page and press coverage of the disclosure.

pin.notes: Not a PIN: a Bluetooth authentication key that, before the 2026-07-20 firmware update, was the same on every KARR-SWDS unit and sat in plain text inside the vendor app. It is product-wide, which is exactly the vulnerability, and it is deliberately not reproduced here — the researchers withheld it, and writing down a working key for 2.2 million cars is not documentation. Whether the patched firmware moves to per-unit keys is not public.

security_advisory.detail: Researchers at UC San Diego reverse-engineered the KARR app and extracted a single Bluetooth authentication key common to ALL KARR-SWDS units. With it, anyone within Bluetooth range (about five yards) can lock and unlock doors, disable the alarm, honk the horn, flash the lights, and immobilize the engine while the car is off. About 2.2 million dealer-installed units are affected — sold through Honda, Toyota, Mazda, Ford and Jeep dealers between 2017 and 2026. The unit also continuously broadcasts an identifiable Bluetooth signal, so its history can reveal where a car has been. Affected cars often carry a "KARR" or "SWDS" sticker on the driver's-side window.

mitigation.summary: Update the alarm's firmware from the KARR app — Acrisure released a patch on 2026-07-20.

security_advisory.summary: Every KARR/SWDS unit shares one Bluetooth key — a nearby attacker can unlock the car, silence the alarm, and immobilize the engine.

credentials.notes: No credential crosses to this app; it never connects.

factory_reset.effect: Not applicable — this app never connects to or configures the device, so it has nothing to reset. Any real reset is done at the device.

methods.description: Passive: the device advertises over BLE, we match the name and warn. No connection is made.

setup.notes: Nothing to set up: this app never connects to the device. It recognises the BLE advertisement and warns; the match is inferred from the advertised name (see testing.notes), hence low confidence.

rejoin.notes: Recognised on sight wherever it advertises; nothing is stored.

testing.notes: Not hardware-verified. The advertisement match (BLE local name starting "KARR" / "SWDS") is inferred from the product and driver's-window sticker names, because the exact BLE device name and service UUID are not public. Treated as low-confidence and WARN-ONLY.
